subsections.section_title: Historical Development and Conceptual Foundations of Resilon
subsections.content:
Resilon emerged in the early 2000s as part of a broader effort to move endodontic obturation beyond the traditional gutta-percha–sealer model toward an adhesive, polymer-based filling system. Its development was closely tied to the Epiphany sealer and a self-etching primer, with the explicit aim of creating a bonded obturation complex that could adapt more intimately to instrumented canal walls and potentially reinforce endodontically treated roots ref [1], ref [2]. This origin reflects a translational logic: concepts from adhesive restorative dentistry were imported into endodontics to address concerns about leakage at sealer–dentin and core–sealer interfaces.

Materially, Resilon represented a substantive innovation rather than a simple reformulation of gutta-percha. It is a thermoplastic synthetic polymer-based core material, commonly described as containing polycaprolactone with bioactive glass, radiopaque fillers, and pigments, designed for use with conventional obturation techniques such as warm vertical compaction and carrier-based delivery while remaining compatible with adhesive sealing strategies ref [1], ref [3]. This combination of handling familiarity and altered chemistry was central to its market and research appeal.

The initial literature framed Resilon as an attempt to create a more integrated root filling system, often discussed in relation to the emerging “monoblock” ideal in endodontics. Early laboratory studies and conceptual reviews therefore focused not only on its composition, but also on whether the new material system could improve sealing and fracture resistance relative to established obturation materials ref [2], ref [4]. In this sense, the innovation of Resilon lay as much in its systems-based rationale as in the polymer core itself.

subsections.section_title: Historical Development and Conceptual Foundations of Resilon
subsections.content:
Conventional obturation paradigms in endodontics have been dominated by gutta-percha used in combination with a sealer, a strategy historically valued for handling characteristics, radiopacity, and retreatability rather than for adhesive integration with dentin. Against this background, Resilon was introduced as a synthetic polymer-based alternative intended to shift obturation from a largely space-filling approach toward a bonded filling concept. This contrasted with the longstanding view that gutta-percha is intrinsically non-adhesive and that sealers primarily compensate for interfacial irregularities rather than create a unified root filling complex ref [5], ref [1].

The comparison therefore centered not only on composition but also on the biological and mechanical assumptions underlying canal filling. Studies comparing leakage and adaptation reported that Resilon/Epiphany could, under some conditions, produce less microleakage than gutta-percha/AH Plus, supporting claims of improved sealing through resin bonding ref [6]. At the same time, broader evaluations of obturation materials emphasized that the clinical success of root filling depends on the combined effects of canal disinfection, dimensional stability, and long-term resistance to degradation, not solely on immediate laboratory sealing outcomes ref [5], ref [7].

Thus, relative to the conventional gutta-percha paradigm, Resilon represented a conceptual reorientation: from an inert core-plus-sealer system toward an adhesive obturation system intended to reinforce the root and reduce coronal-apical leakage. The significance of this comparison in the literature lies in whether such theoretical advantages could meaningfully outperform the durability, familiarity, and retrievability that had made gutta-percha the reference standard ref [1], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Historical Development and Conceptual Foundations of Resilon
subsections.content:
The monoblock concept in endodontics refers to an obturation strategy in which the core material, sealer, and canal dentin are intended to function as a single mechanically integrated unit. In theory, such integration could reduce interfacial gaps, improve stress distribution within the instrumented root, and limit fluid percolation along the filling mass. This idea became central to the rationale for Resilon-based systems, which were introduced not simply as a replacement for gutta-percha, but as part of an adhesive obturation approach designed to create bonding continuity from dentin to sealer to core material ref [1], ref [8].

Tay and Pashley critically framed endodontic monoblocks into primary, secondary, and tertiary forms according to the number of interfaces created within the bonded assembly, highlighting that the Resilon/Epiphany system represented a secondary monoblock rather than a truly interface-free structure ref [4]. This distinction was important because the biological and mechanical success of the concept depended not only on bond formation, but also on the durability of multiple interfaces under moisture, polymerization shrinkage, and functional stress. Subsequent laboratory work showed that although adhesive filling systems could produce measurable bond strength and, in some models, increase resistance to vertical root fracture, these effects were variable and method-sensitive ref [9], ref [10].

Accordingly, the monoblock concept provided the key theoretical foundation for Resilon’s development, but it also exposed the system to scrutiny regarding whether adhesive continuity in the root canal could be predictably achieved in clinical conditions. The later literature on leakage, degradation, and retreatability can be understood as direct tests of this original monoblock proposition.

subsections.section_title: Historical Development and Conceptual Foundations of Resilon
subsections.content:
Resilon was introduced not as a single cone material, but as a multi-component obturation system intended to function cohesively with adhesive endodontic sealers. The core filling material is a thermoplastic synthetic polymer-based cone, formulated primarily from polycaprolactone and containing bioactive glass, radiopaque fillers, and pigments; this composition distinguished it from gutta-percha, which is based on trans-isomerized polyisoprene ref [1], ref [11]. In practical terms, the system was designed to be used with Epiphany sealer and a self-etching primer, so that canal dentin, sealer, and core material would be linked within a single bonded assembly rather than acting as largely discrete phases ref [1], ref [12].

The sealer component was a dual-cure methacrylate resin, while the accompanying primer was intended to condition intraradicular dentin and improve interfacial adaptation under clinically difficult moisture conditions. This architecture reflected the broader "monoblock" rationale: the polymer cone provided thermoplastic handling similar to gutta-percha techniques, whereas the resin sealer/primer complex sought to create adhesion to canal walls and to the Resilon surface itself ref [12], ref [13]. Studies describing the system emphasized that its behavior therefore depended not only on the cone material, but also on polymerization, bonding durability, and the integrity of interfaces throughout the canal space ref [11], ref [13].

Accordingly, the composition and system design of Resilon are central to understanding both its promise and its later controversies. Its synthetic polymer chemistry, filler package, and reliance on resin-based ancillary components represented a substantial departure from conventional zinc oxide-eugenol or epoxy resin sealer/gutta-percha paradigms, and they framed subsequent research on sealing ability, retreatability, biodegradation, and long-term stability ref [1], ref [11], ref [13].

subsections.section_title: Historical Development and Conceptual Foundations of Resilon
subsections.content:
The clinical ambition behind Resilon was to move obturation beyond simple passive canal filling toward a bonded root filling system. In contrast to gutta-percha, which functions largely as an inert core used with a sealer, Resilon was promoted as part of a resin-based obturation complex intended to adhere to dentin and to the sealer, thereby reducing interfacial leakage and improving the long-term seal of the prepared canal ref [1], ref [4]. This objective was closely tied to the broader endodontic goal of entombing residual microorganisms and limiting reinfection through coronal or apical pathways.

A second theoretical advantage was reinforcement of endodontically treated roots. By bonding the core material, sealer, and dentinal wall into a so-called monoblock, the Resilon/Epiphany system was proposed to distribute stresses more evenly and potentially increase resistance to vertical root fracture compared with conventional gutta-percha-based fillings ref [4], ref [14]. This biomechanical rationale was especially attractive in structurally compromised teeth, where preservation of fracture resistance is clinically consequential.

Resilon was also designed to retain practical handling features familiar to clinicians, including thermoplastic delivery and retreatability, while adding adhesive functionality. However, these theoretical benefits depended on durable bonding in the complex root canal environment and on the hydrolytic stability of the resin-based interface, issues that later became central to critical evaluations of the system’s clinical promise ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Material Properties and Physicochemical Characteristics
subsections.content:
Resilon was introduced as a synthetic alternative to gutta-percha, designed around a thermoplastic polymeric core rather than a trans-1,4-polyisoprene matrix. The material has been described as a polycaprolactone-based root filling system containing bioactive glass, radiopaque fillers, and other additives intended to support handling, visibility, and interaction with resin-based sealers ref [1], ref [4]. This chemistry is central to its proposed monoblock concept, in which the core material, methacrylate sealer, and adhesive interface are expected to function as an integrated obturation complex rather than as loosely associated phases ref [4], ref [16].

From a structural standpoint, the semicrystalline aliphatic polyester backbone of polycaprolactone differentiates Resilon from gutta-percha in both thermal response and susceptibility to hydrolytic or enzymatic challenge. Polycaprolactone’s ester linkages confer biodegradability under appropriate conditions, a feature well established in polymer science and later invoked to explain concerns about the long-term stability of Resilon in the root canal environment ref [17], ref [18]. The incorporation of inorganic fillers modifies stiffness and radiopacity, but the composite nature of the material also means that performance depends on filler dispersion and on the integrity of the polymer-filler interface.

Accordingly, the polymer chemistry of Resilon offers theoretical advantages in thermoplastic handling and adhesive compatibility, yet it also introduces vulnerabilities not shared by traditional gutta-percha. The same ester-based chemistry that facilitates processing and blending with resin-oriented obturation strategies may contribute to chemical instability over time, making structural composition a key determinant of the material’s clinical durability ref [1], ref [16], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Material Properties and Physicochemical Characteristics
subsections.content:
Resilon was introduced as a thermoplastic synthetic obturation material intended for use with warm vertical compaction and carrier-based delivery systems. Its polycaprolactone-based matrix softens on heating and can be compacted into canal irregularities in a manner broadly analogous to thermoplasticized gutta-percha, but its flow is governed by a lower softening range and by the presence of bioactive glass, radiopacifiers, and fillers within the polymer phase ref [1], ref [19]. In practical terms, this thermal response was one of the key reasons Resilon could be adapted to continuous-wave and thermomechanical techniques rather than being limited to cold lateral compaction.

Comparative laboratory studies generally indicate that Resilon exhibits flow and thermoplastic deformation compatible with contemporary warm obturation protocols, although its handling is not identical to gutta-percha. The material has shown favorable adaptation to canal walls and accessory anatomy when heat is applied, but excessive heating may also accentuate polymer relaxation and influence post-placement dimensional behavior ref [19], ref [20]. These findings are clinically relevant because the same viscoelastic properties that facilitate penetration into fins and isthmuses can also contribute to stress redistribution and possible shrinkage during cooling.

Flow characteristics must therefore be interpreted together with the sealer-based monoblock concept. Studies of root filling quality have suggested that improved thermoplastic adaptation does not automatically translate into a more stable seal, because interfacial integrity depends on coordinated behavior of the core material, sealer, and dentin under thermal and mechanical cycling ref [20], ref [21]. Accordingly, the thermoplastic advantages of Resilon are best viewed as technique-enabling rather than intrinsically guaranteeing superior long-term sealing performance.

subsections.section_title: Material Properties and Physicochemical Characteristics
subsections.content:
Dimensional stability and solubility are central to the long-term sealing performance of Resilon because even small volumetric changes can compromise adaptation to canal walls and create pathways for leakage. Relative to gutta-percha, Resilon was introduced as a synthetic thermoplastic obturation material intended to function within a bonded obturation concept, but its polymeric nature also raised concern about water sorption and hydrolytic change over time. In comparative evaluations, Resilon has generally shown measurable mass loss and greater susceptibility to fluid-related alteration than conventional gutta-percha, although the magnitude depends on storage medium and test duration ref [22], ref [23].

Laboratory studies of solubility and dimensional change indicate that Resilon is more prone than gutta-percha to degradation-related surface and bulk changes in aqueous environments. Tay et al. demonstrated that components of the Resilon system were vulnerable to hydrolytic and enzymatic challenge, supporting the view that dimensional integrity may deteriorate under clinically relevant conditions ref [24]. Complementary leakage work by Bodrumlu and Tunga also suggested that the stability of the Resilon-based filling complex may be affected by material dissolution and interfacial breakdown over time ref [25].

Taken together, the literature suggests that the dimensional behavior of Resilon cannot be considered independently from its solubility and degradation profile. While initial adaptation may be favorable, long-term stability appears more material- and environment-sensitive than for gutta-percha, particularly in the presence of moisture, alkaline media, or degradative enzymes. This has important implications for the durability of the purported monoblock concept and helps explain why favorable early sealing results have not always translated into superior long-term performance ref [22], ref [24], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Material Properties and Physicochemical Characteristics
subsections.content:
Radiopacity is a prerequisite for any root filling material because postoperative assessment depends on clear discrimination of the filling mass from dentin, cortical bone, and voids on conventional and digital radiographs. For Resilon, radiopacity is primarily achieved through incorporated radiopaque fillers rather than the polycaprolactone-based matrix itself. Comparative studies generally found the material to be radiographically detectable and within accepted endodontic standards, although its opacity may differ from that of conventional gutta-percha formulations depending on specimen thickness and the comparator used ref [26], ref [11].

From a diagnostic perspective, adequate radiopacity supports evaluation of working length control, homogeneity of obturation, detection of underfilled regions, and recognition of overextension. Nevertheless, radiopacity alone does not guarantee superior interpretability: image contrast is also influenced by sealer thickness, projection geometry, and the tendency of highly radiopaque materials to mask internal voids. Experimental radiographic analyses comparing endodontic materials have therefore emphasized that Resilon should be interpreted as part of a material-sealer complex rather than as an isolated cone material ref [26], ref [27].

Clinically, the available evidence suggests that Resilon offers sufficient visibility for routine postoperative imaging, but its diagnostic performance remains technique-sensitive and modality-dependent. This is particularly relevant in retreatment or failure analysis, where differentiation between residual filling material, sealer remnants, and adjacent dentin can be challenging. Thus, radiopacity should be considered an enabling property for radiographic follow-up, but not a surrogate for sealing quality or three-dimensional adaptation ref [11], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Material Properties and Physicochemical Characteristics
subsections.content:
A recurrent concern with Resilon is that its polycaprolactone-based core is not chemically inert in the root canal over long periods. Unlike gutta-percha, the polyester backbone is potentially vulnerable to hydrolytic and enzyme-mediated cleavage, raising the possibility that a material intended to form a bonded obturation complex may gradually lose mass or interfacial integrity. This concern was reinforced by studies showing that Resilon can be degraded by biologically relevant enzymes, particularly esterases and lipases, with measurable surface deterioration and material breakdown under laboratory challenge conditions ref [29], ref [30].

The biodegradation issue is clinically relevant because breakdown need not be extensive to compromise sealing; localized softening, surface pitting, or debonding at the sealer-core interface may be sufficient to create leakage pathways. Tay and coworkers argued that the susceptibility of methacrylate resin-based endodontic obturation systems to hydrolysis and enzymatic attack should be considered alongside their immediate bonding performance, especially in canals where residual moisture, bacterial products, or host-derived enzymes may persist ref [24]. Related work also indicated that microorganisms can colonize and degrade components of resin-based filling systems, providing a biologically plausible route for long-term deterioration when coronal or apical leakage occurs ref [31].

Overall, the literature suggests that Resilon’s biodegradability is a double-edged property: advantageous from a polymer science perspective, but potentially detrimental for permanent root filling. The key implication is that long-term success depends not only on initial adaptation and bond formation, but also on resistance of the polymer-sealer-dentin complex to hydrolytic and enzymatic challenge in the intraradicular environment ref [29], ref [24].

subsections.section_title: Material Properties and Physicochemical Characteristics
subsections.subsection_title: Bonding Interactions with Dentin and Sealers
subsections.content:
A central rationale for Resilon was the creation of a bonded “monoblock” through coupling of the polyester-based core, a methacrylate resin sealer, and conditioned root dentin. In principle, this strategy could reduce interfacial leakage compared with conventional gutta-percha, but the effectiveness of bonding depends on successful smear-layer removal, adequate resin infiltration into radicular dentin, and durable adhesion under the high configuration factor of the canal space. Early laboratory work showed that Resilon used with Epiphany/RealSeal could produce measurable adhesion to intraradicular dentin, although bond strengths were modest and region-dependent, with weaker performance often observed apically ref [32], ref [1].

The sealer–dentin interface is particularly vulnerable because polymerization shrinkage, incomplete light transmission, moisture variability, and limited access for solvent evaporation may compromise hybridization. Push-out and leakage studies therefore reported mixed results: some found improved adaptation or reduced leakage for Resilon-based systems, whereas others demonstrated no clear advantage over gutta-percha-based obturation and highlighted frequent adhesive failures at the sealer–dentin interface ref [1], ref [33]. These findings suggest that the concept of reinforcement by bonded obturation is more difficult to realize clinically than in simplified laboratory models.

Bond durability is further challenged by hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation of resin components and collagen within the hybrid layer. In a review of resin-based obturation systems, Tay and Pashley argued that the methacrylate sealer–dentin bond is susceptible to degradation pathways analogous to those described for coronal dentin bonding, limiting the long-term stability of the purported monoblock ref [4]. Consistent with this concern, comparative evaluations of root reinforcement and dislocation resistance have generally failed to show a robust, lasting mechanical benefit attributable solely to Resilon bonding chemistry ref [33], ref [4].

Overall, the literature indicates that bonding interactions between Resilon, resin sealers, and dentin are chemically plausible but clinically technique-sensitive and biologically unstable. Consequently, interfacial performance appears to depend less on the core material alone than on canal pretreatment, sealer chemistry, curing behavior, and the durability of adhesion in the radicular environment.

subsections.section_title: Biological Performance and Biocompatibility
subsections.content:
Cytotoxicity is a central concern for Resilon-based obturation because the material is intended to function in prolonged contact with dentinal walls while any leachable components may diffuse toward the periapical tissues. In vitro studies generally suggest that Resilon exhibits low to moderate cytotoxicity, often comparable to or lower than some resin-based sealers, but the biological response is strongly conditioned by the accompanying sealer, extraction medium, and duration of aging rather than by the core filling material alone ref [34], ref [35]. This distinction is important when interpreting claims of a so-called monoblock system, since host cells are exposed to the full obturation complex rather than Resilon in isolation.

Cellular assays using fibroblast-like and other mammalian cell lines have shown that freshly mixed methacrylate-containing endodontic materials tend to produce greater reductions in cell viability than set or aged specimens, consistent with the release of unreacted monomers and other soluble components ref [35], ref [36]. Related work on methacrylate resin chemistry in dental materials has identified compounds such as HEMA and TEGDMA as biologically active eluates capable of impairing proliferation, altering redox balance, and modifying cellular metabolism, offering a plausible mechanistic framework for the transient cytotoxic responses reported for resin-based obturation systems ref [37].

Overall, the available evidence indicates that Resilon itself is not uniformly associated with marked cytotoxicity, but its cellular safety profile cannot be separated from the sealer interface and the kinetics of polymerization and degradation. For biological performance, therefore, the more clinically relevant question is not whether Resilon is inert in isolation, but whether the Resilon–sealer complex maintains acceptable cytocompatibility during the early post-obturation period and after long-term aging in a moist environment ref [34], ref [36].

subsections.section_title: Biological Performance and Biocompatibility
subsections.content:
Periapical tissue compatibility is a critical benchmark for Resilon-based obturation because any sealer or core material extruded beyond the apex may directly contact periodontal ligament, bone, and inflammatory cells. The available evidence suggests that Resilon systems are broadly tolerated, but their biological acceptability depends heavily on the accompanying sealer rather than on the polyester-based core alone. In a subcutaneous implantation model, both Resilon and gutta-percha elicited only mild to moderate connective-tissue reactions that diminished over time, supporting the view that the core material itself is not markedly aggressive to host tissues ref [38].

At the periapical level, however, compatibility must also be interpreted in light of degradation behavior and sealing durability. Tay et al. showed that Resilon is susceptible to enzymatic and hydrolytic degradation, raising the possibility that breakdown products or interfacial deterioration could compromise long-term tissue compatibility indirectly by permitting leakage and persistent apical irritation ref [24]. This concern is biologically relevant because persistent periapical inflammation is often driven less by bulk material toxicity than by microbial penetration through a failing root filling.

Animal and implantation studies on methacrylate resin–based endodontic sealers reinforce this qualified interpretation. Epiphany-type sealers have generally shown an initial inflammatory response that decreases with time, but not clear superiority over established gutta-percha/sealer combinations in tissue compatibility ref [39], ref [40]. Accordingly, the current literature supports Resilon as a material with acceptable short-term periapical biocompatibility, while emphasizing that long-term host response is inseparable from sealer chemistry, material stability, and resistance to apical leakage.

subsections.section_title: Biological Performance and Biocompatibility
subsections.content:
From an antimicrobial perspective, Resilon was introduced partly within a monoblock concept intended to reduce leakage pathways and thereby limit residual or recurrent infection. However, available evidence suggests that any antimicrobial benefit is indirect rather than intrinsic. In an ex vivo leakage model using polymicrobial challenge, roots filled with Resilon/Epiphany exhibited delayed bacterial penetration compared with gutta-percha/AH Plus, although leakage still occurred over time, underscoring that obturation material alone does not sterilize the canal system ref [41].

Direct antimicrobial activity of Resilon-based systems appears limited. Studies examining the Epiphany sealer associated with Resilon have generally shown weaker antibacterial effects than epoxy resin–based sealers such as AH Plus, particularly against Enterococcus faecalis, a species frequently implicated in persistent endodontic infection ref [42]. This is consistent with broader in vitro evaluations indicating that antibacterial performance among sealers is material-dependent and often transient, reflecting initial release of reactive components rather than sustained bioactive inhibition ref [43].

A further concern is durability: the polycaprolactone-based Resilon core is susceptible to hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation, and microbial lipases or esterases may contribute to surface deterioration, potentially compromising the long-term seal and creating conditions favorable to recolonization ref [44]. Thus, the antimicrobial significance of Resilon should be framed primarily in terms of sealing performance and its stability over time, not as a substitute for thorough chemomechanical disinfection.

subsections.section_title: Biological Performance and Biocompatibility
subsections.content:
From an immunobiological perspective, Resilon should be assessed not only as a core filling polymer but as part of a sealer–monoblock system whose degradation products and interfacial leakage may influence host response. Short-term implantation and cytocompatibility studies generally suggested that Resilon-based obturation systems do not elicit uniquely severe reactions compared with conventional gutta-percha/sealer combinations, although the response remains strongly dependent on the associated sealer chemistry rather than on the thermoplastic cone alone ref [6], ref [45].

Evidence from subcutaneous implantation models indicates that methacrylate resin–based endodontic materials can provoke an initial inflammatory infiltrate that tends to diminish over time as the material becomes encapsulated, but persistent irritation may occur when unreacted monomers or degradation by-products are present ref [46]. This is clinically relevant because hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation of the Resilon system has been documented, raising the possibility that long-term material breakdown could sustain low-grade periapical irritation even if early tissue compatibility appears acceptable ref [47].

Accordingly, the immune profile associated with Resilon is best interpreted as conditionally acceptable rather than intrinsically bioinert. Current literature does not support a distinctive pro-inflammatory advantage over established obturation approaches; instead, inflammatory outcomes appear to depend on sealing integrity, extrusion, and the biological behavior of the companion resin sealer. These considerations help explain why favorable handling or bonding claims have not consistently translated into clear biological superiority in vivo ref [6], ref [47].

subsections.section_title: Biological Performance and Biocompatibility
subsections.content:
The concept of bioactivity in obturation systems extends beyond passive sealing to whether the material can support mineral deposition, maintain a favorable interfacial environment, and avoid impairing periapical repair. Resilon was introduced as part of a methacrylate-based obturation system intended to create a bonded “monoblock,” but this design goal is not equivalent to intrinsic bioactivity. In contrast to calcium silicate–based materials that can release calcium ions and promote apatite formation, the available literature positions Resilon primarily as a synthetic thermoplastic polymer with acceptable handling and sealing aspirations rather than a material with strong, direct hard-tissue inductive potential ref [1], ref [48].

Experimental work has nevertheless suggested some capacity for surface mineral interaction under favorable conditions. Tay et al. reported that polycaprolactone-based root-filling materials may undergo hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation, a finding relevant because degradation can alter the local interface and compromise the stability required for tissue healing ref [24]. Related in vitro observations by Hiraishi et al. showed that the methacrylate resin-based sealer used with Resilon could exhibit incomplete polymerization in the root canal environment, which may further limit the long-term integrity of the bonded interface needed for predictable periapical repair ref [49].

Accordingly, the healing potential of Resilon appears to depend less on active stimulation of regeneration and more on whether the system preserves an adequate seal and remains biologically tolerable over time. Reviews comparing contemporary endodontic biomaterials generally place Resilon below bioactive hydraulic cements in terms of regenerative promise, while acknowledging that satisfactory healing may still occur when microbial control and canal disinfection are achieved ref [48], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Sealing Ability, Mechanical Performance, and Clinical Functionality
subsections.content:
Apical and coronal microleakage has been central to claims that the Resilon/Epiphany system can create a more effectively sealed root filling than gutta-percha–based obturation. Early laboratory work using fluid-filtration and bacterial-leakage models suggested that, when combined with a resin sealer and self-etch primer, Resilon could reduce leakage relative to conventional gutta-percha/sealer combinations, supporting the concept of a bonded obturation complex ref [51], ref [1]. These findings were particularly influential because they linked reduced tracer or bacterial penetration to the material’s proposed adhesive interaction with dentin and the core material.

However, subsequent evidence has been less uniform. Comparative leakage studies have shown that the apparent advantage of Resilon is highly method-dependent and may diminish after aging, thermocycling, or prolonged storage, indicating that any initial improvement in sealing is vulnerable to hydrolytic and interfacial degradation ref [6], ref [52]. Reviews of leakage methodology also caution that dye, fluid, and bacterial models are not interchangeable and often produce different rankings for the same materials, limiting strong conclusions about superiority from any single test paradigm ref [53].

Overall, the literature supports a nuanced interpretation: Resilon may achieve low early apical and coronal leakage under controlled conditions, but a consistent long-term sealing advantage over gutta-percha has not been demonstrated. Thus, microleakage outcomes should be interpreted alongside data on adaptation, bond durability, and clinical aging rather than as standalone proof of improved endodontic performance.

subsections.section_title: Sealing Ability, Mechanical Performance, and Clinical Functionality
subsections.content:
Interfacial adaptation is central to the proposed advantage of the Resilon/Epiphany system, which was designed to create a bonded obturation complex rather than a purely mechanically retained filling. Early microscopic and leakage-oriented studies suggested that Resilon-based fillings could adapt closely to dentinal walls when the self-etch sealer infiltrated the conditioned canal surface, but this idealized “monoblock” has proved difficult to achieve consistently in clinical geometries because polymerization shrinkage, high configuration factor within root canals, and technique sensitivity can generate interfacial gaps and internal porosities ref [1], ref [54].

Void formation has been documented both within the core-sealer mass and at the dentin-sealer interface, with outcomes strongly influenced by placement method and canal morphology. Micro-computed tomography and related imaging studies have shown that neither Resilon nor gutta-percha systems are void-free, and that irregular, oval, or flattened canals remain especially vulnerable to unfilled recesses despite thermoplastic techniques ref [55]. In comparative analyses of root filling quality, the extent and distribution of voids often depended more on obturation technique than on the core material alone, tempering claims that Resilon intrinsically yields superior adaptation ref [55], ref [56].

From a clinical standpoint, these findings imply that any potential bonding benefit of Resilon must be interpreted cautiously. Interfacial defects may provide pathways for fluid ingress and may also compromise stress transfer across the filling-dentin interface over time. Thus, adaptation with Resilon appears feasible but not uniformly reliable, especially where moisture control, sealer polymerization, and complex canal anatomy challenge formation of a continuous bonded interface ref [54], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Sealing Ability, Mechanical Performance, and Clinical Functionality
subsections.subsection_title: Fracture Resistance of Endodontically Treated Teeth
subsections.content:
A central rationale for Resilon-based obturation was the possibility of creating a bonded “monoblock” that might reinforce structurally compromised roots. Early laboratory studies supported this concept, reporting higher resistance to vertical root fracture in teeth filled with Resilon/Epiphany than in teeth obturated with gutta-percha and conventional sealers under static loading conditions [1,2]. These findings were interpreted as evidence that adhesion between the filling material, sealer, and dentin could distribute stresses more favorably than nonbonded filling systems.

However, the reinforcing effect has not been uniformly reproduced. Subsequent in vitro work showed that any gain in fracture resistance was modest and strongly dependent on specimen preparation, remaining dentin thickness, irrigation regimen, and loading design; in some models, Resilon performed similarly to gutta-percha-based controls rather than providing a clear mechanical advantage [3,4]. This inconsistency suggests that the intrinsic weakening caused by instrumentation and access preparation may outweigh the contribution of the obturation material itself.

From a clinical perspective, fracture resistance data for Resilon should therefore be interpreted cautiously. Most evidence derives from ex vivo tests using monotonic compressive loading, which incompletely simulate fatigue, occlusal cycling, and long-term hydrolytic degradation at the adhesive interface. Accordingly, while Resilon may improve fracture resistance under selected experimental conditions, current evidence does not establish a durable or clinically decisive reinforcement effect in endodontically treated teeth [3,4].

subsections.section_title: Sealing Ability, Mechanical Performance, and Clinical Functionality
subsections.subsection_title: Push-Out Bond Strength and Adhesion Testing
subsections.content:
Push-out bond strength testing has been widely used to interrogate the adhesive behavior of Resilon/Epiphany systems within root dentin, because it applies a predominantly shear-dominated dislodgement load to obturation slices and can differentiate performance along coronal, middle, and apical levels. In principle, Resilon was introduced to create a so-called monoblock through bonding between the synthetic polymer core, methacrylate-based sealer, and conditioned canal dentin; however, experimental findings have generally shown only modest or inconsistent bond strength values, with marked sensitivity to irrigation regimen, smear layer management, and regional dentin variability ref [1], ref [62].

Comparative studies indicate that the adhesion of Resilon-based fillings is often not uniformly superior to gutta-percha/sealer controls when assessed by push-out methods. In particular, hybrid layer continuity and resin tag formation may be compromised by polymerization shrinkage, limited light access in the canal, hydrolytic degradation, and the unfavorable cavity configuration factor of the root canal space, all of which can concentrate stresses at the sealer–dentin interface ref [1], ref [63]. These factors help explain why bond values may decline toward the apical third and why failure modes frequently include mixed or adhesive failure rather than cohesive failure within the core material.

Methodologically, interpretation of push-out data requires caution because specimen thickness, plunger diameter, canal taper, and storage conditions can substantially alter measured values. Nonetheless, the broader adhesion-testing literature suggests that while Resilon can achieve measurable bonding to intraradicular dentin, this interface is technique-sensitive and may not provide a consistently durable mechanical advantage under clinically relevant aging conditions ref [62], ref [64].

subsections.section_title: Sealing Ability, Mechanical Performance, and Clinical Functionality
subsections.content:
The performance of Resilon-based obturation is particularly sensitive to canal anatomy because the material is typically used with thermoplasticized or carrier-based techniques intended to improve adaptation in irregular spaces. In principle, this may benefit oval, ribbon-shaped, or accessory canal systems where cold lateral compaction often leaves unfilled recesses. However, anatomy-driven gains in adaptation do not necessarily translate into a more durable seal, because the quality of the interface remains dependent on smear layer removal, sealer polymerization, and the configuration factor within long, narrow canals ref [65], ref [1].

Micro-computed tomography and sectioning studies of root fillings have shown that canal shape strongly influences the persistence of voids and untouched extensions regardless of filling material, with oval canals posing a particular challenge to complete obturation ref [66]. In this context, Resilon may show better mass flow into fins or broader buccolingual extensions when heat-softened, but its advantages are constrained by the same geometric limitations that affect gutta-percha-based systems. Comparative work in complex canal configurations has therefore generally suggested technique sensitivity rather than anatomy-independent superiority, especially in canals with high ovality or irregular isthmus-containing cross-sections ref [66], ref [67].

Clinically, this means that Resilon should be viewed less as a universal solution for difficult anatomy than as a material whose performance depends on how well the selected delivery method matches canal morphology. In straightforward round canals, outcomes may resemble those of conventional obturation, whereas in wide oval or anatomically complex canals, improved flow must still be paired with careful shaping, irrigation, and sealer management to minimize void formation and preserve functional sealing over time ref [1], ref [67].

subsections.section_title: Sealing Ability, Mechanical Performance, and Clinical Functionality
subsections.subsection_title: Longevity of Seal Under Functional Conditions
subsections.content:
The longevity of a Resilon-based seal under functional conditions depends on whether the initial adhesive interface can resist hydrolytic degradation, thermal stress, and cyclic occlusal loading over time. Early enthusiasm for the so-called monoblock concept was tempered by evidence that favorable immediate sealing does not necessarily translate into durable interfacial stability. In particular, long-term fluid filtration and leakage studies have shown that the sealing performance of Resilon/Epiphany may deteriorate after aging, suggesting vulnerability of the resin sealer–dentin and sealer–core interfaces to water sorption and degradation ref [68], ref [69].

A major concern is the biodegradation of the polyester-based core material and associated resin components in moist endodontic environments. Tay et al. demonstrated that methacrylate resin-based sealers are susceptible to degradation by esterases and hydrolysis, providing a mechanistic basis for loss of seal over time under clinical conditions ref [24]. Complementing this, studies of Resilon specifically reported surface and structural degradation when exposed to alkaline and enzymatic challenges, indicating that the material may not remain dimensionally and chemically stable throughout long-term service ref [70].

Clinically, these durability issues are consistent with outcome data showing no clear long-term superiority of Resilon over gutta-percha-based obturation. In a randomized clinical trial with follow-up after primary root canal treatment, Conner et al. found comparable healing outcomes for Resilon and gutta-percha rather than improved success with the resin-based system ref [71]. Taken together, current evidence suggests that while Resilon can provide an acceptable short-term seal, its long-term functional reliability is constrained by interfacial and material aging phenomena.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Techniques, Retreatment, and Comparative Effectiveness
subsections.content:
Resilon was introduced as a thermoplastic synthetic polymer-based core material intended for use with resin sealers to create a bonded “monoblock” within the prepared root canal. Clinically, it was designed to be handled with techniques already familiar from gutta-percha obturation, including cold lateral compaction, warm vertical compaction, carrier-based delivery, and thermomechanical approaches, with adaptation governed by the associated Epiphany/RealSeal sealer and primer steps rather than by a fundamentally different shaping philosophy ref [1], ref [72].

In practice, most reports describe Resilon obturation as beginning with conventional canal preparation and drying, followed by application of a self-etching primer and dual-cure methacrylate resin sealer before insertion of Resilon cones or heat-softened material. This sequence makes the technique more moisture- and time-sensitive than traditional zinc oxide–eugenol or epoxy-resin/gutta-percha protocols, because polymerization, dentin wetness, and sealer thickness influence adaptation and interfacial continuity ref [1], ref [73]. Warm vertical compaction and System B/Obtura-style delivery were promoted to improve filling homogeneity, while single-cone use was generally tied to greater dependence on sealer properties and canal taper matching.

Experimental comparisons suggested that Resilon could be used with the same broad obturation armamentarium as gutta-percha, but technique selection remained closely linked to goals of maximizing canal wall adaptation and minimizing leakage. Laboratory studies on root filling quality and leakage therefore framed Resilon less as a wholly new obturation method than as a material system whose clinical performance depended heavily on meticulous execution of adhesive obturation steps ref [72], ref [74].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Techniques, Retreatment, and Comparative Effectiveness
subsections.content:
Clinical use of the Resilon/Epiphany system was introduced as a protocol intended to create a bonded obturation complex, but its performance is notably technique-sensitive. Unlike conventional gutta-percha with nonadhesive sealers, the protocol requires coordinated canal conditioning, application of a self-etching primer, careful sealer placement, and controlled delivery of the thermoplastic core material. Tay et al. emphasized that the concept depends on maintaining adhesion across the dentin–primer–sealer–core interfaces, making the system more vulnerable to errors in substrate preparation and polymerization than traditional obturation approaches [1].

A recurring practical issue is moisture control and smear layer management. Because resin-based adhesion in the root canal is challenged by residual irrigants, limited access, high C-factor geometry, and variable dentin wetness, small deviations in clinical steps may reduce interfacial integrity. In particular, studies examining the so-called monoblock concept argued that polymerization shrinkage, incomplete infiltration, and the complexity of bonding to radicular dentin can compromise the continuity originally claimed for the system [2]. These concerns help explain why operator consistency and strict adherence to manufacturer instructions are especially important when Resilon is used.

Technique sensitivity is also reflected in filling quality. In a micro-computed tomography study, Zmener and Pameijer showed that procedural variables influenced void formation and adaptation even when contemporary warm obturation methods were used with the Resilon/Epiphany SE system [3]. Clinically, this suggests that successful use depends not only on material selection but also on meticulous canal drying, thin and uniform sealer application, and familiarity with heat and compaction parameters to avoid sealer pooling, stripping, or interfacial disruption.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Techniques, Retreatment, and Comparative Effectiveness
subsections.content:
Retreatment is a critical test of any obturation system because successful nonsurgical revision depends on effective removal of the filling mass and re-establishment of canal patency. For Resilon/Epiphany systems, the intended bonded monoblock concept raised early concern that adhesion to dentin might hinder retreatment; however, experimental studies generally indicate that the material can be removed with conventional retreatment approaches, including rotary NiTi instruments and solvent-assisted techniques, although complete elimination from canal irregularities remains difficult, as with gutta-percha-based fillings ref [77], ref [78].

Comparative laboratory work has suggested that Resilon may be removed more rapidly than gutta-percha in some protocols, particularly when rotary retreatment files are combined with chloroform or other solvents, but these time advantages do not necessarily translate into cleaner canal walls or less residual debris ref [77], ref [79]. Micro-computed tomography and split-root evaluations consistently show remnants of both materials in fins, isthmuses, and oval extensions after retreatment, underscoring that anatomical complexity, rather than bulk material type alone, is the main determinant of residual filling material ref [78], ref [80].

From a clinical standpoint, the retreatability of Resilon appears acceptable but technique-sensitive. Heat-softened carrier-based forms and deeply penetrated sealer tags may complicate removal, and supplementary irrigation, ultrasonic activation, or further apical enlargement may be required to improve cleanliness. Thus, Resilon should not be regarded as irretrievable, yet current evidence does not show that it confers a decisive retreatment advantage over established gutta-percha systems ref [79], ref [80].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Techniques, Retreatment, and Comparative Effectiveness
subsections.subsection_title: Interaction with Irrigants and Intracanal Medicaments
subsections.content:
Because Resilon is used with a methacrylate-based sealer, its interaction with irrigants and medicaments is more technique-sensitive than conventional gutta-percha systems. In particular, oxidizing irrigants can compromise polymerization and interfacial bonding if residues remain on canal walls. Studies evaluating Epiphany/Resilon have shown that sodium hypochlorite alone may adversely affect sealer adhesion, whereas final irrigation protocols that remove the smear layer and reduce oxygen-rich residues can improve bonding conditions, especially when EDTA is incorporated as a final rinse ref [81], ref [82].

The effect of intracanal medicaments is similarly important. Calcium hydroxide residues are difficult to eliminate completely and may interfere with sealer penetration into dentinal tubules and with the continuity of the Resilon–sealer interface. Experimental work has indicated that prior calcium hydroxide dressing can reduce the bond strength of Resilon/Epiphany to root dentin when medicament remnants persist, reinforcing the need for meticulous canal debridement before obturation ref [83].

A related issue is the use of chlorhexidine. Although chlorhexidine lacks the oxidizing effect of sodium hypochlorite and may be attractive as a final irrigant, the broader adhesive endodontic literature suggests that its benefits are protocol-dependent rather than universal. Overall, the available evidence supports a practical sequence in which smear layer removal and thorough drying are prioritized, and in which both irrigant carryover and medicament remnants are minimized to preserve the intended monoblock-like behavior of the Resilon system ref [82], ref [84].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Techniques, Retreatment, and Comparative Effectiveness
subsections.content:
Comparative studies between Resilon/Epiphany and gutta-percha–based obturation systems have generally focused on sealing ability, resistance to leakage, and reinforcement of instrumented roots. Early laboratory work proposed that the Resilon system could create a so-called “monoblock,” with improved resistance to bacterial or fluid penetration relative to conventional gutta-percha with sealer; this concept was supported in initial leakage and fracture-resistance reports, although these findings were largely derived from in vitro models with substantial methodological heterogeneity ref [6], ref [85].

Subsequent direct comparisons, however, have yielded a more cautious interpretation. Systematic review evidence indicates that Resilon has not shown a consistent or clinically decisive advantage over gutta-percha across leakage, bond strength, or physical performance outcomes, in part because results vary with canal preparation, irrigation regimen, sealer chemistry, and aging protocol ref [86]. Long-term durability has been a particular concern, as hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation of resin-based components may compromise the integrity of the interface over time, reducing any early laboratory benefit relative to established gutta-percha techniques ref [87].

From a comparative effectiveness perspective, the literature therefore suggests functional equivalence or only context-specific advantages rather than clear superiority of Resilon over gutta-percha systems. This has important clinical implications: when judged against the simplicity, familiarity, and long-term track record of gutta-percha, Resilon appears to offer limited incremental benefit despite its initially attractive adhesive rationale ref [86], ref [1].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Techniques, Retreatment, and Comparative Effectiveness
subsections.content:
Clinical outcome evidence for Resilon-based obturation remains limited relative to the extensive laboratory literature, and the available human studies have not demonstrated a clear superiority over gutta-percha–based approaches. In a prospective randomized clinical trial, Shipper et al. reported high short-term healing rates for both Resilon/Epiphany and gutta-percha/AH Plus, with no statistically significant difference in success, suggesting that any proposed monoblock-related advantage did not translate into an obvious clinical benefit within the follow-up period ref [88].

Observational outcome data point in the same direction. In a retrospective study of endodontic outcomes after single-visit treatment, both Resilon and gutta-percha performed similarly, and the dominant determinants of healing were conventional biological and technical factors rather than the core material itself ref [89]. More broadly, reviews synthesizing the early clinical literature concluded that evidence supporting improved periapical healing or tooth survival with Resilon was weak and insufficient to justify claims of superior long-term effectiveness ref [1].

This cautious interpretation is reinforced by systematic review-level assessments of root filling materials, which have generally found inadequate high-quality clinical evidence to favor newer synthetic obturation systems over established gutta-percha/sealer combinations ref [90]. Accordingly, the clinical literature positions Resilon as a viable alternative obturation material, but not one with proven outcome advantages in routine endodontic practice.

subsections.section_title: Limitations, Controversies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A persistent difficulty in interpreting the Resilon literature is that conclusions vary markedly across study designs. Early laboratory work, often using push-out, leakage, or fracture-resistance models under tightly controlled conditions, suggested that the Epiphany/Resilon system could create a more integrated root filling complex and in some settings improve resistance to vertical root fracture relative to gutta-percha-based controls ref [91], ref [92]. However, these advantages were not consistently reproduced when different irrigation regimens, sealer thicknesses, storage conditions, or loading protocols were used, indicating that apparently favorable findings were highly model-dependent.

The divergence becomes more pronounced when in vitro studies are compared with biological and aging-oriented investigations. Microbial leakage and biodegradation studies raised concerns that Resilon and its methacrylate sealer interface may be vulnerable to hydrolytic and enzymatic deterioration over time, undermining the long-term significance of short-term sealing data ref [93], ref [94]. Thus, a material may perform well in immediate bond-strength or leakage experiments yet appear less robust in models that incorporate thermocycling, prolonged water storage, or bacterial challenge.

Clinical evidence has remained comparatively limited and has not clearly confirmed a durable superiority over conventional obturation. This mismatch between promising bench-top outcomes and less decisive long-term relevance reflects broader translational problems in endodontic materials research: surrogate endpoints are easier to measure than patient-centered success, but they do not necessarily predict it. For Resilon, conflicting evidence across study types therefore reflects not only inconsistent results, but also fundamental differences in what each experimental design is actually capable of demonstrating.

subsections.section_title: Limitations, Controversies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Challenges in Evaluating Obturation Materials
subsections.content:
A central methodological problem in evaluating Resilon and other obturation systems is the heterogeneity of experimental endpoints. Studies alternately prioritize dye or fluid leakage, push-out bond strength, bacterial penetration, micro-CT void analysis, or fracture resistance, yet these outcomes are not interchangeable proxies for clinical success. The lack of standardized canal anatomy, irrigation regimens, smear-layer management, storage media, and aging protocols makes cross-study comparison difficult and can invert apparent material rankings. This concern is reinforced by broad critiques of leakage models and by the variable predictive value of laboratory bond-strength tests for endodontic performance ref [95], ref [96].

Another challenge is that material behavior is highly technique-sensitive. Resilon was designed to function as part of a bonded obturation concept, so performance depends not only on the core material but also on the compatible sealer, primer application, canal moisture, and polymerization conditions. In practice, many comparative studies differ in operator experience, obturation technique, and retreatment or post-space preparation protocols, introducing confounding that is difficult to isolate from intrinsic material properties. Reviews of laboratory testing in Endodontology have therefore emphasized the need for better-controlled, clinically relevant models and clearer reporting standards ref [96], ref [97].

A further limitation is temporal compression: many investigations assess immediate sealing or bond values after short storage periods, whereas hydrolytic degradation, enzymatic challenge, and thermomechanical fatigue may be more relevant to long-term reliability. Longitudinal aging studies have shown that resin-based root filling systems can lose interfacial integrity over time, underscoring the inadequacy of short-term in vitro endpoints as stand-alone evidence ref [98]. Future evaluations should integrate standardized aging, microstructural imaging, and prospective clinical outcomes to determine whether laboratory advantages translate into durable therapeutic benefit.

subsections.section_title: Limitations, Controversies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A persistent concern in the Resilon literature is whether its proposed monoblock concept can withstand the chemically aggressive and biologically variable conditions of the root canal over time. Unlike gutta-percha, the polyester-based core and resin sealer are potentially susceptible to hydrolytic and enzymatic attack, raising the possibility that initially favorable interfacial adaptation may deteriorate during function. This concern was sharpened by evidence that microorganisms can degrade Resilon components, suggesting that long-term sealing may depend not only on immediate bond formation but also on resistance to biodegradation within residual or recurrently infected canals ref [99].

Durability studies have reinforced this uncertainty. Aging protocols involving water storage, thermocycling, or leakage testing have often shown that the sealing advantage claimed for Resilon is reduced or lost with time, indicating that bond stability may be less durable than early short-term experiments implied. In particular, long-term leakage evaluations reported progressive deterioration in fluid-tightness for both Resilon/Epiphany and conventional fillings, with no durable superiority of the synthetic system ref [100]. Related work on disassembly and retreatment also suggests that the sealer-core interface does not behave as a permanently integrated structure under clinical manipulation, further questioning the practical meaning of a monoblock under long-term service conditions ref [77].

Taken together, the degradation profile of Resilon highlights a broader translational problem: short-term laboratory bonding does not necessarily predict long-term clinical reliability. Future studies should therefore prioritize clinically relevant aging models, interfacial nanoleakage under cyclic stress, and direct comparisons between material degradation and treatment outcomes, rather than relying primarily on immediate bond-strength endpoints ref [101].

subsections.section_title: Limitations, Controversies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
Despite early enthusiasm that Resilon/Epiphany might create a bonded “monoblock,” routine clinical adoption remained limited and appears to have declined over time. This pattern likely reflects the gap between favorable laboratory claims and more cautious evidence from translational and clinical studies. In a practice-based comparison, the short-term outcomes of Resilon did not clearly surpass those of gutta-percha-based obturation, reducing the incentive for clinicians to change familiar protocols ref [102]. Likewise, broad reviews of root-canal filling materials have noted that the proposed advantages of resin-based obturation were not matched by compelling long-term clinical superiority ref [103].

Adoption was also constrained by technique sensitivity and concerns about durability. Resilon systems required additional adhesive steps, moisture control, and compatibility across sealer–core interfaces, all of which complicated use relative to conventional gutta-percha. At the same time, reports of hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation of polyester-based materials raised doubts about whether the initial seal could be maintained over time ref [104]. These practical and biological concerns likely weakened clinician confidence, especially when balanced against the familiarity, retrievability, and lower cost of established obturation systems.

The subsequent commercial decline of Resilon therefore illustrates a broader translational lesson in endodontic biomaterials: laboratory demonstrations of interfacial bonding are insufficient if they do not yield reproducible clinical benefit, manageable handling, and durable service performance. For next-generation obturation materials, clinical uptake will depend not only on improved sealing concepts but also on simplified delivery, predictable retreatability, and robust outcome data from adequately powered comparative studies ref [2,4].

subsections.section_title: Limitations, Controversies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
The Resilon experience offers an important design lesson for next-generation obturation systems: improving immediate interfacial bonding is insufficient if the material is vulnerable to hydrolytic, enzymatic, or microbial degradation over time. The promise of a bonded “monoblock” was conceptually attractive, but evidence that methacrylate-based sealers can undergo polymerization stress and that resin–dentin bonds in root canals are difficult to stabilize under clinical conditions suggests that future materials must prioritize long-term interfacial durability rather than short-term adhesion alone ref [106], ref [107].

A second implication is that future materials should be developed as integrated chemomechanical systems rather than as isolated filling cores. This includes compatibility with irrigants, residual moisture, dentin substrate heterogeneity, and retreatability requirements. Contemporary bioceramic sealers illustrate a different design philosophy: instead of relying on polymeric bonding, they emphasize dimensional stability, bioactivity, and favorable interaction with dentin moisture, while also introducing new questions about disassembly and clinical handling ref [108], ref [109]. The trajectory away from Resilon therefore reflects not only product-specific shortcomings, but also a broader shift toward materials that tolerate the endodontic environment rather than attempt to fully polymer-bond it.

For future innovation, the key target may be multifunctionality: antimicrobial persistence without cytotoxic compromise, resistance to biodegradation, predictable retreatability, and validated performance in aging models that better approximate long-term service. In this respect, lessons from Resilon argue for stricter translational pathways in which laboratory claims of sealing, reinforcement, or monoblock behavior are tested against clinically relevant aging, leakage, and failure endpoints before widespread adoption ref [107], ref [110].

subsections.section_title: Limitations, Controversies, and Future Research Directions
subsections.content:
A central research gap is the absence of robust, long-term comparative clinical evidence. Much of the Resilon literature is dominated by laboratory leakage, bond-strength, or fracture-resistance models whose endpoints are only indirect surrogates for healing and tooth survival. Future work should prioritize adequately powered pragmatic trials and prospective registries using standardized outcomes such as periapical healing, retreatability, postoperative disease, and restoration-adjusted tooth survival, rather than relying primarily on short-term in vitro proxies ref [111], ref [112].

A second priority is methodological harmonization. Reviews of root-canal obturation studies have highlighted major heterogeneity in specimen selection, irrigation regimens, aging protocols, leakage models, and statistical reporting, which makes cross-study synthesis difficult and may partly explain contradictory findings. Consensus test standards should include thermo-mechanical aging, enzymatic or hydrolytic degradation challenges, and interfacial characterization at multiple time points to better simulate the clinical environment and to clarify whether any initial monoblock effect is durable ref [112], ref [113].

Finally, future material development should move beyond the original Resilon concept toward obturation systems designed for chemical stability, bioactivity, and predictable retreatability. Evidence that methacrylate resin-based sealers can absorb water and undergo hydrolytic degradation underscores the need for polymers and interfaces that remain dimensionally and chemically stable in moist canals over years, not weeks ref [114]. In this sense, Resilon should be viewed less as a settled solution and more as a useful case study for defining performance benchmarks for next-generation endodontic materials ref [111], ref [114].
